_comment: Four shock cards. 'tape' is passed straight to runTape(). 'expect' is checked against the live engine by test/content.contract.test.js, so the teacher lines can never drift from the model.

experiments.title: You raise rates, and hold
experiments.subtitle: Policy rate up one point in Q1, held for two years
experiments.teacherLine: Markets have moved. The real economy has not responded yet.
experiments.setup: You are the central bank. Inflation is at target and growth is steady, and you raise the rate anyway. Watch which parts of the screen move in the first quarter and which do not.

watchFor.say: Yield up, dollar up, equities down about five and a half points. Growth and inflation both still read 2.00. Nothing in the real economy has happened.
Look at the credit tile. Current 100. Target 95.6. Nothing has happened yet, and something certainly will. That gap is the lag.
Credit starts to tighten. Growth and inflation have barely moved.
Growth has slid towards 1.6 and inflation follows more slowly, into the high 1.7s. It took a year and a half.

experiments.askTheClass: Equity fell in Q1. Open the attribution panel. Which term did the most damage, and which contributed exactly nothing?
experiments.answer: The discount rate did most of it, at minus 3.37. Credit contributed exactly zero, because credit has a one-quarter lag and had not moved yet.

experiments.title: Energy supply is cut
experiments.subtitle: Energy up ten points in Q1, held, and the bank does nothing
experiments.teacherLine: A physical shock, two layers down, arriving as inflation a quarter later.
experiments.setup: A disruption takes energy supply out of the system and it does not come back. The policy rate stays where it is. This is the shock that starts in the physical economy rather than the financial one.

watchFor.say: Energy jumps almost ten points. Equities fall. Yields tick up because expected inflation rose. Printed inflation is still exactly 2.00.
Inflation prints 2.24. Growth starts to feel the cost.
Inflation near 2.8 with growth near 1.55. That is stagflation in miniature: prices up and output down at the same time.

experiments.askTheClass: Compare the equity attribution with the rate-rise card. Same fall, different reason. What changed?
experiments.answer: In the rate rise, the discount rate did the damage. Here the discount rate barely moved; energy costs and weaker expected growth did it instead. Same direction, different cause, so a different policy would be needed.

experiments.title: You raise rates, then change your mind
experiments.subtitle: Up one point in Q1, back to the starting rate in Q3
experiments.teacherLine: The lag runs both ways. Undoing a decision takes as long as making it.
experiments.setup: Run the rate rise, then reverse it after two quarters. The point is not that the reversal works. The point is how long it takes to show up.

watchFor.say: Identical to the held card so far. The reversal has not happened yet.
The rate is back to 3.50 today, but credit is still tightening from a decision taken two quarters ago.
Credit is recovering, near 99.5 against 94.9 if you had held. Growth is climbing back. The damage was real and it is being undone at the same speed it arrived.

experiments.askTheClass: In the quarter you reversed, did anything in the real economy improve?
experiments.answer: No. Markets repriced immediately, but credit, growth and inflation carried on moving in the old direction, because they read decisions from previous quarters.

experiments.title: The same shock, with the bank on a rule
experiments.subtitle: Energy up ten points, and the central bank reacts automatically
experiments.teacherLine: Now you are not the central bank. The rule is, and it responds to its own effects.
experiments.setup: Run the energy shock again, but hand the rate to the rule. Compare it with the card where the bank did nothing.

watchFor.say: The rule raises the rate towards 3.9 straight away, on expected inflation, before any inflation has printed.
Equities take a deeper mark than when the bank sat still: about 92.9 against 95.3. The class is paying for the response as well as the shock.
The rate dips. Ask why before explaining.
Growth is weaker than in the do-nothing run, and inflation is only a little lower. Rates cannot make energy less scarce.

experiments.askTheClass: In Q2 the bank cuts, in the quarter that inflation first printed higher. Is that a mistake?
experiments.answer: No, it is arithmetic. The rule reads expectations, and expectations already contain the rate it set last quarter, so its own first move argues part of itself away. It is a real feature of rules that react to their own effects, and worth naming out loud rather than hiding.
